PROVENANCE, 29 July 2026. This file was first written on a worktree branched
from main, where docs/ASK-PROTOCOL.md did not exist, so its shapes were the
ones the M4 brief and TRAY-DESIGN section 3 describe. It has since been
CORRECTED against the real thing: src/commands/setup-channel.ts and
src/wizard/steps.ts as they stand on the ask branch. Three of the guesses
were wrong and all three mattered:
the answer form is `answer <id> <json value>`, three fields separated by
spaces, NOT a JSON envelope carrying the id
the question's prose is on `prompt`, not `message`, and every ask also
carries a STABLE `name`, which is a far better thing to match a scripted
answer on than a sentence somebody may reword
a refused answer produces `answer-refused` and the question STAYS LIVE. It
is not re-asked, so a driver waiting for a second ask event waits forever
Where this file and the code disagree the code wins and this file is the
bug. Every scenario that depends on a shape the build does not speak yet
SKIPS with a sentence rather than failing.
How the rig decides whether the thing in front of it is an M4 build at
all. Both are questions asked of the build rather than of a version
string: a version says what somebody typed, --help says what shipped.
The setup channel. `-c` is not decoration: it is the only thing standing
between this rig and the real ~/.photo-pigeon on this machine, so the rig refuses
to run setup at all unless the built CLI declares it. See the safety
block at the top of run-m4.ps1.
$noOpenFlag: Prints the console deep links instead of handing them to a browser.
Passed when the build declares it, because a rig that opens six Google
Cloud tabs on somebody's desktop is a rig nobody runs twice. When it is
absent the rig still runs, and says in its output that a browser may have
$answerForm: The one payload-carrying form M4 is allowed to add, and it is a form
rather than a seventh word. Two shapes were written for M4 by different
hands and only one can exist on a wire. Checked against
The payload is JSON either way, so a string carries its quotes and its
escapes: it is where a Windows path lives and the backslashes have to
survive. The other shape is named rather than forgotten because a rig
that hardcodes a grammar is a rig that lies about which one it tested.
Everything else on the core's stdin is still one of the six bare words,
and setup answers none of them but stop and quit.
$maxAttemptsPerAsk: A refused answer leaves the question LIVE and is not re-asked, so a rig
that answers once and waits waits forever. The driver answers again when
a refusal names a question it answered, and gives up after this many
tries with the refusal's own sentence in the report. Without the cap a
genuinely invalid answer becomes an infinite loop between two programs

$comment: `configured` carries `written: false` when the user kept the config that
was already on disk, which is a different thing from a setup having
written one. The rig checks the field when it is there.
The field names on an `ask` event. Named here rather than inline in the
rig so that a protocol which spells `kind` as `type` costs one edit.
`name` is the one to match a scripted answer on: it is a stable
identifier the wizard chose, where `prompt` is prose somebody may reword
between milestones. The answer script tries the name first and falls back
to the prose, so this rig reads a build that has names and one that does
not.
`error` is on no event this protocol emits. It is kept because the rig's
driver reads a re-ask carrying one as a second attempt, which is the
other shape a channel like this can take, and reading both costs nothing.
askFields.name: name

$comment: A refusal names the question it is about when it has one, and carries a
sentence fit to show a person.
The shipped core answers EVERY answer line on one event type, an
`answered` carrying `accepted`. The receipt for a good answer and the
refusal of a bad one are therefore the same event with a different
verdict, and `accepted` is the whole of the difference. A driver that
counts a receipt as a refusal answers a question that is already closed,
then answers the refusal of that, until the attempt cap saves it.
`detail` and `error` are both read, because the two M4 protocols spelled
the sentence differently and reading both costs one line.
The scripted answers, matched in order, first match wins. `kind` is
'confirm', 'input', 'pick' or 'any'. `name` is an exact match against the
ask's stable name and is tried FIRST, because a name is chosen and a
prompt is prose. `match` is a regex tested against the prompt, case
insensitively, and is what answers a build whose asks carry no name.
`value` is either a literal or one of the substitution tokens below,
which the rig fills in from the run directory it made.
{watchDir}         the throwaway folder the fake photos land in
{credentialsPath}  a synthetic client JSON in the sandbox, never real
{projectId}        a made up Google project id
{albumName}        the album name, the same one the other rigs use
The last two rules are the catch-all, and they are the reason a wording
change in the wizard does not break this rig: an unmatched confirm takes
the question's own default, an unmatched input answers empty. Both are
recorded in the report so a run that fell through to them can be read
afterwards rather than trusted.

$comment: doctor --json against the throwaway environment. `ok` is the verdict and
`checks` is the list; the rig reads both and reports every check that is
not ok by name, because 'doctor is red' with no line number is a bug
report nobody can act on.
Green here means ok:true, which is 'no check FAILED'. Notes and warnings
are expected and are printed rather than counted against the run: a
throwaway setup has never signed in, so 'Not signed in yet' is a warning
the rig should read and not a failure it should hide.
The first-run window, and how a script can make one exist without a
hand on the mouse.
The trigger is not a test-only back door and that is deliberate: a tray
that starts and finds NO config is exactly the machine the M4 exit
criterion describes, and opening the first-run window is what it is
supposed to do. So the rig points PHOTO_PIGEON_CONFIG at a path in a
temp directory where no file exists, launches, and waits for a window.
openEnv is the escape hatch: if the shell grows a variable or a flag that
opens a named window on launch, name it here and the rig uses it instead
of relying on the no-config path. Neither is required for the rig to
refuse safely: with no window at all every window scenario skips.

$comment: The handle count probe TRAY-DESIGN asks for at the end of section 6:
'164 fresh against 415 after a day, which is worth confirming settles
rather than climbing once the menu has been rebuilt a few thousand
times'. Windows arriving at M4 is the moment that question stops being
theoretical, so the rig opens and closes one three times and watches the
shape of the line rather than its height.
The FIRST open is not a leak and must never be scored as one. The same
A/B in section 6 measured what it is: the Windows shell and UI stack
mapping in, 54 modules the fresh process did not have, paid once. So the
probe scores the SLOPE AFTER the first cycle, and records the one-off
separately as evidence for the row in section 6 that M4 owns.
$perCycleTolerance: Handles per open/close cycle, averaged over the cycles after the first.
Twelve is deliberately loose: the number that matters is whether the line
is flat or climbing, and a probe that fails on three handles of noise
gets switched off within a week. A real leak of one window's worth of
handles is tens to hundreds per cycle and this catches it easily.

$comment: The RAM row TRAY-DESIGN section 6 leaves explicitly unfilled for M4:
'the first-run window open RAM row is explicitly unfilled and belongs to
M4'. The rig fills it by measuring rather than by reasoning.
Project decision: the budget is about PRIVATE working
set, 15 MB target and 25 MB reopen. Total working set stays an
observation and is never a trigger, because 28 of the 32 megabytes in
section 6's table are Windows' own file-backed pages and this app does
not control one of them.
The webview processes are measured and recorded and are NOT scored. They
are Microsoft's runtime rather than this project's binary, no budget has
ever been agreed for them, and inventing one inside a rig is how a
number nobody agreed to ends up gating a release.
The project rule about the happy toast, in the form
the rig can check.
'First ever' means the ledger was empty before that delivery. It is
core-owned truth and it travels on the event. The shell-owned flag file
is DELETED as a migration, so the rig asserts its ABSENCE from
shell-state.json: a shell still keeping its own count is a shell that can
